name: Tang Dynasty

fields.foundation: The Tang Dynasty was founded in 618 CE by Li Yuan (Emperor Gaozu), Duke of Tang and a Sui military commander at Taiyuan. The Sui had been brought down by Emperor Yang's disastrous campaigns against the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo (the Goguryeo–Sui War) and the massive rebellions they provoked. Li Yuan used the collapse to seize the capital Chang'an in 617 and proclaimed a new dynasty the following year. The founding was a family enterprise. Li Yuan's second son, Li Shimin, was the decisive commander in the campaigns that secured the dynasty, and in 626 staged the Xuanwu Gate Incident, an ambush in which he killed his brothers, the crown prince Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji, before compelling his father to abdicate in his favour. As Emperor Taizong (r. 626–649), Li Shimin presided over what Chinese tradition celebrates as a golden age of humane government, military power and cultural creativity. On the frontier, rather than simply excluding the steppe peoples, Taizong incorporated Turkic and other non-Han peoples into the Tang military and administrative system. After the defeat of the Eastern Turks in 630 he was acclaimed 'Heavenly Khagan' by their chieftains, a recognition that the Tang empire straddled the Chinese and Inner Asian political worlds. Empress Wu Zetian (r. 690–705) interrupted the Tang line by proclaiming her own Zhou dynasty. The long reign of Emperor Xuanzong (r. 712–756) followed, and Chinese historians regard his Kaiyuan era (713–741) as the Tang's cultural and administrative peak. By the census of 754 the registered population stood at roughly 53 million, and Chang'an was among the largest and most cosmopolitan cities on earth.
fields.socioeconomy: At its peak the Tang economy was among the most developed and commercially integrated in the world. Its agricultural base was organised under the equal-field (juntian) system of land allocation, and it was connected to transcontinental trade through the overland Silk Road and the maritime routes of the South China Sea. Chang'an, with perhaps a million inhabitants within and around its walls, was a cosmopolitan commercial centre: Sogdian, Persian, Arab, Indian, Korean, Japanese and Central Asian merchants traded in its two great markets, exchanging silk, ceramics and Chinese manufactures for horses, spices, aromatics, glassware and luxury goods from across Eurasia. The equal-field system, which allocated land to adult males in return for tax and labour obligations, provided a relatively stable agricultural base in the early and middle Tang. It broke down progressively as aristocratic and monastic estates absorbed land and reduced the state's ability to allocate holdings to new households. Woodblock printing developed during the Tang and was used chiefly for Buddhist texts and calendars; the Diamond Sutra of 868, found at Dunhuang, is the oldest surviving dated printed book, though the commercial potential of printing would not be fully realised until the Song. In the An Lushan Rebellion (755–763) the frontier general An Lushan rose with his northeastern armies, captured Luoyang and Chang'an and forced Xuanzong to flee to Sichuan. The rebellion completed the collapse of the equal-field system and devastated much of northern China. In 780 the dynasty replaced the old per-capita levies with the two-tax system based on property, but it remained dependent on increasingly autonomous regional military governors (jiedushi) whose fiscal independence permanently reduced imperial revenues.
fields.military: In the early and middle Tang the dynasty's armies were among the strongest in the world. They combined the disciplined infantry and cavalry traditions of the Chinese agricultural core with the steppe cavalry skills of Turkic, Sogdian and other Inner Asian commanders and soldiers taken into imperial service. The fubing militia system, inherited from the Northern Zhou and Sui and refined by the early Tang, provided a force of farmer-soldiers whose service obligations were linked to land allocation, sparing the state the cost of a large permanent professional army. The early Tang campaigns ranged widely. The Eastern Turkic Khaganate was destroyed in 630 and Gaochang conquered in 640, and under Taizong's successor Gaozong the defeat of the Western Turkic Khaganate in 657 extended Tang suzerainty across the Tarim Basin and into Transoxiana, bringing Chinese power to its greatest westward extent. The Battle of Talas in 751, where a Tang army under Gao Xianzhi was defeated by Abbasid forces after the defection of its Karluk allies, is often cited as marking the limit of Tang westward expansion, and is traditionally linked with the transmission of paper-making westward through captured craftsmen. By the 730s and 740s the fubing had decayed and been replaced on the frontiers by large professional armies under military governors. The An Lushan Rebellion (755–763) showed that these frontier armies, professional, regionally rooted and loyal to their commanders, were both more powerful than any force the court could raise and politically uncontrollable. After 763 the dynasty depended increasingly on regional commanders whose loyalty could not be reliably compelled, and on palace armies controlled by eunuchs. The balance between the imperial centre and regional power-holders never returned to that of the early Tang.
fields.governance: Tang government was among the most developed administrative systems of the medieval world. It was built on the structure of three departments and six ministries (sansheng liubu), which became the template for Chinese imperial administration for centuries. The three departments, the Secretariat, the Chancellery and the Department of State Affairs, divided policy-making into successive stages of drafting, review and implementation, so that imperial edicts were subject to genuine institutional scrutiny before taking effect. The six ministries, Personnel, Revenue, Rites, War, Justice and Works, administered the branches of government through hierarchical bureaucracies whose officials were drawn from aristocratic families and, in growing numbers, from the civil service examinations, especially the prestigious jinshi degree. Taizong's relationship with his ministers, particularly the remonstrating official Wei Zheng, whose blunt criticisms the emperor famously accepted, became a model of sagely government that Chinese political thought idealised for centuries. The Tang Code, first issued in 624 and supplemented in 653 by an authoritative official commentary (Tang Lü Shuyi), was a comprehensive legal compilation that influenced the legal systems of Japan, Korea and Vietnam, and so carried Tang institutions across East Asia. The collapse of central authority after the An Lushan Rebellion forced the dynasty to accept the entrenchment of the jiedushi, regional military governors who controlled taxation, appointments and armies in their provinces. At court eunuchs came to dominate the palace armies and the succession, as the failed attempt to purge them in the Sweet Dew Incident of 835 showed. This quasi-feudal decentralisation was never reversed, and it led to the Five Dynasties period that followed the dynasty's fall.
fields.impact: The Tang Dynasty's historical impact came through several channels at once: the commercial integration of Eurasia along the Silk Road, the cultural and institutional influence of Tang China on its East Asian neighbours, and technological developments, including printing, refined ceramics and the earliest known gunpowder formulas recorded by Tang alchemists, that would eventually change world history. Chang'an in the early and middle Tang had few equals anywhere in its cosmopolitanism. Nestorian Christians, Zoroastrians, Manichaeans and Buddhists maintained temples and monasteries in the capital, alongside communities of Muslim merchants, while the state employed Sogdian financiers, Turkic generals, Korean officials and scholars from Japan. The Tang tributary order drew Japan, the Korean kingdoms and other neighbours into a hierarchical diplomatic framework of periodic missions to Chang'an. These missions transmitted Chinese administrative models, writing, Buddhist institutions and material culture, with consequences that long outlasted the dynasty. Japan's Taika Reform (645) and Taihō Code (701) explicitly modelled themselves on Tang institutions, and Japanese embassies to the Tang carried monks and students who brought Tang learning home. Unified Silla absorbed Tang administrative law, Confucian learning and Buddhist culture. In the Red River delta, governed under the Tang as the Protectorate of Annam from 679, Tang rule left deep institutional and cultural marks before Vietnam secured its independence in 939. Ceramic technology reached a classical maturity under the Tang, with the white Xing wares, the three-colour (sancai) glazed wares and the painted wares of Changsha, which reached markets across the Islamic world and East Africa and established Chinese ceramics as a prestige commodity in world trade.
fields.decline: The Tang Dynasty declined through a long structural deterioration, marked by the catastrophe of the An Lushan Rebellion and ending in the warlordism of the late ninth century. The rebellion of 755–763 was the turning point. The registered population fell from about 53 million to under 17 million, a collapse that reflected both mass mortality and the breakdown of household registration. The equal-field system disintegrated, the militarily autonomous jiedushi rose to power and central fiscal authority was permanently weakened. The Huang Chao Rebellion (874–884), a great uprising led by a former salt smuggler, sacked Luoyang in 880 and Chang'an in 881 and was the final blow. It destroyed much of what remained of the institutions of central government, killed great numbers of the educated elite who staffed the bureaucracy, and transferred effective power to warlords who used the crisis to consolidate regional dominance. The last Tang emperors were puppets of competing warlords, and the dynasty's formal end came in 907 when Zhu Wen, a former lieutenant of Huang Chao who had defected to the Tang and risen to dominate the court, deposed the last emperor and founded the Later Liang. The ensuing Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period (907–960) was a prolonged political fragmentation, yet it preserved much of the Tang institutional and cultural inheritance and encouraged the commercial and agricultural developments that the Song would systematise. What the Tang left behind, its administrative templates, legal codes, literary culture, Buddhist institutions and commercial networks, was so thoroughly embedded in East Asian civilisation that later Chinese dynasties defined themselves as its heirs, and its influence on Japan, Korea and Vietnam continued long after the dynasty itself had fallen.
fields.summary: Under the Tang Dynasty Chinese imperial cosmopolitanism was at its height. Chang'an stood at the centre of a wide Eurasian world, drew talent, commerce and culture from across the continent and spread Chinese institutional and cultural models across East and Southeast Asia, with consequences that persist to the present day.
fields.teaser: The Tang Dynasty is often considered China's golden age, when Chang'an, with perhaps a million inhabitants, was among the world's largest cities and a cosmopolitan centre of art, poetry and international trade.
fields.t0: Founded in 618, the Tang Dynasty pushed Chinese power deep into Central Asia and made Chang'an one of the world's great cities.
fields.t1: Its law code, government model and Buddhist culture were adopted by Japan, Korea and Vietnam and shaped East Asia for centuries.
fields.t2: The An Lushan Rebellion left power with regional generals; the Huang Chao uprising finished it and a warlord deposed the last emperor in 907.
fields.dyk: The Diamond Sutra of 868, found at Dunhuang, is the oldest surviving dated printed book in the world.
